blocks.html:
⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

Every certificate in the platform — edge TLS, Linkerd mesh identity, internal server and admin certs, and the client certificates issued to end users — chains back to one in-cluster CA managed by cert-manager. This page walks the issuer chain resource by resource, shows how trust-manager distributes the resulting trust bundle to every consumer, and explains where Let's Encrypt takes over on cloud deployments.

The issuer chain

The chain lives in k8s/opendefence-pki/ and is applied to the cert-manager namespace during infra-phase3 (cert-manager itself installs in phase 1, trust-manager in phase 2 — see Deployment model). The ClusterIssuer resources are cluster-scoped, but their secretName references resolve in the cert-manager namespace, which is why the CA Certificates are pinned there.

Resource Name What it does
ClusterIssuer selfsigned-issuer Bootstrap issuer (selfSigned: {}) — exists only to sign the root.
Certificate ca-cert The root CA. isCA: true, ECDSA P-256, O=PVARKI. CN is localmaeher Root CA on local; on cloud it is templated to <DEPLOYMENT> Root CA, where <DEPLOYMENT> is the Zarf variable OPENDEFENCE_DEPLOYMENT (the first DNS label of the deployment host). Keypair lands in Secret ca-secret.
ClusterIssuer ca-issuer Signs with ca-secret.
Certificate intermediate-ca The working intermediate. isCA: true, ECDSA P-256, duration: 43800h (~5 years). CN localmaeher Intermediate CA / <DEPLOYMENT> Intermediate CA. Keypair lands in Secret intermediate-ca-secret.
ClusterIssuer intermediate-ca-issuer Signs with intermediate-ca-secret — issues effectively all leaf certificates.

Both Certificates are defined per overlay (overlays/local/ and overlays/cloud/) because their subjects differ; selfsigned-issuer, ca-issuer and the trust bundle sit in base/, while intermediate-ca-issuer is declared alongside the intermediate Certificate in each overlay file.

Two branches hang off the chain:

  • Mesh identity: ca-issuer (the root, not the intermediate) also signs Certificate linkerd-identity-issuer in the linkerd namespace, the CA Linkerd uses to mint workload identities — issuer mechanics and rotation are on the Service mesh page.
  • Everything else: intermediate-ca-issuer issues the internal server leaves and, through rmapi, the end-user client certificates described below. Server leaves include rmui-tls/rmui-mtls-tls and the wildcard-opendefence-dev wildcard on local, and tak-server-admin on both local and cloud — a client certificate with CN tak.<domain> that takrmapi uses against the TAK admin API.

One inconsistency: two server leaves skip the intermediate and are issued directly by ca-issuer — the local keycloak Certificate (keycloak-tls, serving kc.<domain>:9443) and the openldap Certificate (openldap-tls, in both overlays) — so those chain straight to the root.

The full chain, resource by resource:

blocks.html:
Trust distribution

Issuing certificates is only half the job — every verifier needs the CA public certs. That is trust-manager's role. Bundle ca-bundle (defined next to the chain in k8s/opendefence-pki/base/ca-bundle.bundle.yaml) concatenates the public halves of ca-secret and intermediate-ca-secret and syncs the result into every namespace, as both a ConfigMap and a Secret named ca-bundle:

apiVersion: trust.cert-manager.io/v1alpha1
kind: Bundle
metadata:
  name: ca-bundle
spec:
  sources:
  - useDefaultCAs: false
  - secret: {name: "ca-secret", key: "tls.crt"}
  - secret: {name: "intermediate-ca-secret", key: "tls.crt"}
  target:
    configMap:
      key: "ca-cert.pem"
    secret:
      key: "ca.crt"

useDefaultCAs: false means the bundle contains only this deployment's CAs — it is a verification bundle for platform-internal identities, not a general internet trust store. Syncing to Secrets is an opt-in trust-manager feature; the Helm values (k8s/trust-manager/base/kustomization.yaml, chart v0.20.2) enable secretTargets with authorizedSecrets: [ca-bundle]. Because the bundle lands in every namespace automatically, a new integration namespace gets the CA for free — no copying secrets around.

The consumers:

Consumer How it gets the bundle
rmapi OS trust store The shared kustomize Component k8s/_shared/rmapi-container-init mounts container-init.sh (ConfigMap rmapi-container-init-hack — the name is honest, the repo calls it a hack) which copies the bundle from /pvarki-ca/opendefence-ca-cert.pem into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ and runs update-ca-certificates.
Keycloak Mounts the ConfigMap at /trust and sets KC_TRUSTSTORE_PATHS=/trust/ca-cert.pem — the truststore used to validate client certificates for --https-client-auth=request (built into the pvarki/keycloak-server image) on its own TLS port 9443.
Traefik edge mTLS TLSOptions mtls-optional and mtls-strict reference the Secret target (clientAuth.secretNames: [ca-bundle], key ca.crt) to verify end-user client certs — see Edge mTLS & callsign checks.
Product containers Products mount the bundle for their own trust needs (conventionally at /ca_public); e.g. the TAK pod's certs-handler init container runs split-ca.sh to split it back into root_ca.pem and intermediate_ca.pem for TAK's keystores.
Linkerd trust anchors A second, separate Bundle, linkerd-identity-trust-roots, sources only ca-secret (the root alone) and targets a ConfigMap (key ca-bundle.crt) restricted by namespaceSelector to the linkerd namespace. With identity.externalCA: true, Linkerd reads its trust anchors from there.

blocks.html:
End-user client certificates

The same chain issues the personal client certificates that end users present at the mTLS edge. rmapi acts as the certificate authority front end, with cert-manager as the signing backend, configured through environment in the opendefence-system kustomization:

RBAC is deliberately narrow: the rmapi ServiceAccount is bound to a namespaced Role (k8s/opendefence-system/base/resources/rmapi.role.yaml) granting create, get, list, watch, delete on certificaterequests.cert-manager.io in opendefence-system — rmapi can request and collect signed certificates, but never touches the CA Certificates or key Secrets.

When an enrollment is approved, rmapi creates a CertificateRequest whose CN is the user's callsign, referencing intermediate-ca-issuer. cert-manager signs it with the intermediate key and writes the certificate back into the request's status; rmapi collects it and hands the user a bundle (certificate, private key, CA chain). These are exactly the certificates the Traefik edge later validates against ca-bundle on the mtls.<domain> and product hosts — the enrollment UX and the edge-side callsign checks are covered on Edge mTLS & callsign checks.

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant rmapi
    participant certmanager as cert-manager
    participant Traefik

    User->>rmapi: Enrollment approved, callsign assigned
    rmapi->>certmanager: Create CertificateRequest (CN = callsign, issuer intermediate-ca-issuer)
    certmanager->>certmanager: Sign with intermediate-ca-secret key
    certmanager-->>rmapi: Signed certificate in CertificateRequest status
    rmapi-->>User: Bundle with client cert, private key and CA chain
    User->>Traefik: TLS handshake presenting the client cert (mtls host)
    Traefik->>Traefik: Verify chain against ca-bundle Secret (TLSOption)
    Note over Traefik: Callsign validity checks follow, see the edge mTLS page

blocks.html:
Public certificates on cloud

Browsers will not trust the internal root, so cloud deployments add ACME. infra-phase2 on cloud applies k8s/cert-manager-clusterissuers/, which defines two ClusterIssuers: letsencrypt-http01-staging and letsencrypt-http01-production (HTTP-01 solver with ingressClassName: traefik, ACME account benjam@opendefence.fi).

The cloud overlays then request production Let's Encrypt certificates for the browser-facing hosts — e.g. rmui-tls for the root <domain>, rmui-mtls-tls for mtls.<domain>, plus keycloak, grafana, tak, mtx, battlelog and the Matrix hosts (matrix, synapse-server, mas, matrix-rtc). Even the mTLS hosts serve a publicly trusted server certificate on cloud; what stays internal is client verification — the TLSOptions keep pointing at ca-bundle, so only certificates from the in-cluster chain are accepted as client identities. The internal CA also continues to sign the Linkerd identity issuer, tak-server-admin, openldap-tls, and all end-user client certificates on cloud.

The staging issuer is defined but currently unreferenced by any manifest — it exists so bring-up experiments can avoid Let's Encrypt production rate limits. On local (kind) there is no ACME at all: every server certificate comes from the internal chain, so browsers warn unless you import the local root.

Lifetimes, rotation and revocation pointers

Certificate Lifetime Notes
ca-cert (root) no explicit duration — cert-manager's default (90 days) applies A default-lifetime root above a 5-year intermediate is a known rough edge.
intermediate-ca 43800h (~5 years) Signs virtually all leaves.
linkerd-identity-issuer 48h, renewBefore: 25h Short-lived by design; see Service mesh (Linkerd).
Let's Encrypt leaves (cloud) ACME-standard ~90 days Renewed automatically by cert-manager.
End-user client certs set by rmapi at request time Not declared in this repo's manifests.

Rotation procedures (what to do when the root or intermediate approaches expiry, and how renewals propagate through trust-manager) belong to Day 2 operations (Kubernetes). For revocation, see the known limitation on the Edge mTLS page.
